title: Alaska Drawing Permits Explained (No Points, Pure Lottery)
excerpt: Alaska has no preference or bonus points. Here's how its drawing permit lottery works for moose, caribou, sheep, goat, bison and bear, plus fees, nonresident limits, guide rules, Tier II and registration permits.
content:
Alaska doesn't use points of any kind. Every drawing permit hunt is a fresh lottery each year: a first-time applicant has exactly the same chance as someone who has applied for twenty years. You can't build toward a hunt, but you also can't fall behind. And a lot of Alaska hunting needs no draw at all. Many moose, caribou, sheep and deer hunts run on a free harvest ticket, and registration permits are usually unlimited.

So when people ask how Alaska's "points" work, the honest answer is: they don't exist. What matters is choosing hunts wisely, using all your applications, and, for nonresidents, lining up a guide when the species requires one.

How you get into the drawing

There's nothing to buy ahead of time except a license and the application fee.

  • Window: one application period a year, November 1 at 8 a.m. to December 15 at 5 p.m. Alaska time. You apply in late fall for hunts in the regulatory year that starts the next July 1. The current window, November 1 – December 15, 2026, is for 2027–28 hunts.
  • License first: you need an Alaska hunting license to apply ($45 resident, $160 nonresident). Residents 17 and younger don't need one. A license for the current year or the hunt year works.
  • Application fees: $5 per application for moose, caribou, brown bear, black bear, elk, mountain goat and Dall sheep. $10 for bison and muskox ($20 for a bison party). Fees aren't refunded, and applications are online only.
  • Locking tags: nonresidents don't buy the species locking tag to apply. You buy it before you hunt.
  • No point-only option. There's nothing to accumulate.

How the drawing works

Each hunt has its own random drawing. Here's what you control:

  • Up to six applications per species. That count includes party applications. Go over six for a species and ADF&G rejects all of them.
  • Repeat entries: you can apply for the same hunt more than once, which gives you more chances in that hunt. A few hunts limit this, such as guided nonresidents on Kodiak brown bear.
  • Parties: two hunters can apply together and share one draw number. If either is ineligible, the whole application is thrown out. Two nonresidents hunting with a resident relative can't apply as a party.
  • Results: posted the third Friday of February.

Nonresident limits

There's no statewide nonresident quota. Instead, the Board of Game sets nonresident access hunt by hunt:

  • Resident-only and nonresident-only hunts. The supplement lists who can apply. Some hunts are split into guided and unguided versions.
  • Percentage caps on some sheep hunts. For Dall sheep drawing hunts such as the Tok Management Area and Delta Controlled Use Area, the Board has allocated about 10% of permits to nonresidents (20% in Unit 13D, per a 2016 Board summary). Check the current supplement for each hunt.
  • Hunting with a relative. Kodiak brown bear hunts cap nonresidents guided by resident relatives at four per season and eight per regulatory year.

Guide requirements for nonresidents

Nonresidents who are U.S. citizens must hunt brown/grizzly bear, Dall sheep and mountain goat with an Alaska-licensed guide or a resident relative 19 or older within the second degree of kindred (parent, sibling, child, spouse, grandparent, grandchild, in-laws and step-relatives). Nonresident aliens need a guide for every big game species.

For a guided drawing hunt, you need a signed guide-client agreement before or at the time you apply, and your guide's verification code goes on the application. Book the guide first, then apply. Drawing a permit doesn't guarantee a guide.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Rules after you draw

There are no points to lose, but there are limits that work like waiting periods:

  • One drawing permit per species per regulatory year.
  • No back-to-back wins on the exact same hunt. You can't be awarded the same drawing hunt two years in a row, unless permits went undersubscribed.
  • Bison: a resident who wins a bison permit can't apply for another for 10 years. A nonresident who wins can't apply again.
  • Kodiak: hunters drawn for a fall Kodiak bear hunt can't draw a Kodiak permit the next spring.
  • Report or sit out. If you don't report on a permit, you can't get permits the next year.
  • Each species is separate. Moose, caribou, sheep, goat, bison, brown bear, black bear and elk each get their own six applications and their own one-permit limit.

Tier I, Tier II and registration permits

Tier II permits are subsistence hunts for Alaska residents only, used when there isn't enough game for everyone. They're not random. Applications are scored on five questions about your history with the game population and the cost of food and fuel where you live, up to 140 points, and permits go to the highest scores. Ties are broken at random. Tier II uses the same November–December window and February results.

Tier I and community subsistence hunts are also resident-only. The Unit 13 Nelchina caribou Tier I hunt and the Copper Basin community caribou hunt aren't being held in 2026–27. For 2027–28, ADF&G announced in September 2026 that a Nelchina caribou Tier II hunt (TC566) may be offered; watch the upcoming subsistence supplement.

Registration permits aren't a draw. They're usually unlimited and issued online or in person during a set window, but the hunt can close early by emergency order once the harvest quota is reached. Many brown bear and some moose hunts work this way.

"Points to draw" without points

With no points, odds come down to permits divided by applicants, every year. There's no creep, but popular hunts stay long shots forever.

Moose example (illustrative): a hunt offers 5 permits and draws 500 applications. Each entry has about a 1% chance. Apply once a year for 10 years and you have roughly a 1-in-10 chance of drawing at least once. Use all six moose applications across several similar hunts and your yearly odds rise.

Deer example (no draw): Alaska's Sitka black-tailed deer hunts are general season hunts. You buy a license (and a nonresident deer tag) and go. No draw.

Strategy

  • Use all six applications for each species you want. At $5 each, it's cheap.
  • Apply where demand is low. Remote, hard-to-reach hunts often draw fewer applicants.
  • Don't wait on a draw. Plan a general season moose or caribou hunt or a registration bear hunt while you apply.
  • Nonresidents: guide first. For brown bear, sheep and goat, your guide often knows which draw hunts they hold permits for and helps you apply.
  • Watch the budget. Fly-in costs dwarf tag fees. See discount guided hunts for deals.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Does applying every year help? Only in that each year is another chance. There are no points, so last year's application doesn't improve this year's odds.

Can I apply for the same hunt more than once? Yes, as long as your total for that species stays at six or fewer.

Is there a nonresident quota? Not statewide. Some hunts are resident-only, and the Board of Game has historically allocated nonresidents a small share (about 10%) of some sheep drawing permits. Check the current supplement for each hunt.

Do I need a guide to apply? For guided hunts of brown bear, sheep and goat, yes: the signed contract and guide code must be in place by the time you apply.

Can nonresidents apply for Tier II? No. Tier I and Tier II hunts are for Alaska residents only.

title: Arizona Bonus Points Explained (Elk & Deer)
excerpt: How Arizona's bonus point system works for elk and deer: extra random numbers for each point, the 20% bonus pass, the 10% nonresident cap, loyalty and hunter education points, PointGuard, and how points are lost.
content:
Arizona uses a bonus point system. Every application gets a random number, and each bonus point you hold gives you one more random number. The computer uses your best (lowest) number. On top of that, up to 20% of the tags in each hunt are set aside for the applicants with the most points. So points help a lot, but they never guarantee a tag, and a lucky applicant with zero points can still draw a premium hunt. That's very different from a pure preference point state, where the top point holders always draw first.

Points are tracked by genus: you build elk points and deer points separately. Deer points cover both mule deer and Coues whitetail.

How you get bonus points

  • Apply and miss. Submit a valid application for elk or deer and don't draw, and you earn one point for that genus. Rejected applications don't count.
  • Buy a point only. Use the bonus-point-only hunt number as your only choice: 3000 for elk (February draw) or 1000 for deer (June draw). It costs just the application fee, $13 resident or $15 nonresident, plus a hunting license if you don't already have one.
  • License first. You must hold an Arizona hunting or combination license valid through the deadline day. Nonresidents pay $160 for the combination hunt and fish license; residents pay $37 (hunting) or $57 (combination). Youth 10–17 pay $5. Licenses are valid for one year from purchase.
  • Age: You must be 10 by the application deadline.
  • Limit: One point per genus per draw. Leftover first-come tags neither use nor earn points.

Two extra points

  • Loyalty point. Apply for a genus (for a tag or a point) at least once a year for five years in a row and you earn one loyalty point for that genus. You keep it as long as you keep applying every year. Miss one year and it's gone.
  • Hunter education point. Graduating from an Arizona hunter education course, or the department's online conservation education course, earns one permanent point for each genus. The online course, Ethically Hunting Arizona, is for hunters 18 and older and costs $150 for residents or $300 for nonresidents. You must pass it at least 30 days before a draw deadline for the point to count in that draw. You can only earn this point once.

How points are used in the draw

You can list up to five hunt choices. The draw runs in three passes, with fresh random numbers each time:

  1. Bonus pass. Up to 20% of each hunt's tags (one tag in hunts with 2–4 tags) go to applicants who listed that hunt as their first or second choice, starting with the highest point total. If more applicants at the top point level want the hunt than there are tags, random numbers decide. Then the next point level, and so on.
  2. First and second choice pass. The rest of the tags are drawn by random number among first- and second-choice applicants.
  3. Third, fourth and fifth choice pass. Any tags still left go to applicants who listed them lower.

In every pass, your application gets one random number plus one more for each point, including loyalty and hunter education points. Only your lowest number is used.

Groups: Two to four hunters can apply together. The group's points are the average of everyone's points, rounded to the nearest whole number (.5 rounds up). A group draws only if there are enough tags for everyone, and if one member is rejected, the whole group is rejected.

The nonresident cap

For bull elk and antlered deer, nonresidents can draw no more than 10% of a hunt's tags, rounded down. In hunts with 10 or fewer tags, nonresidents can get one at most, and a hunt with a single tag is resident-only. No more than half of the nonresident tags can be issued in the bonus pass. The Game and Fish Commission can raise nonresident numbers in a hunt to meet management goals.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Keeping and losing points

  • Drawing resets that genus to zero. Draw an elk tag and your elk points are used up. Your loyalty point (if you keep applying) and hunter education point stay.
  • Five years without applying for a genus wipes out its bonus points.
  • Skipping any year costs you the loyalty point for that genus.
  • Buying a surrendered tag that the department reissues also uses up your points.
  • No waiting period. You can apply again the year after you draw.

PointGuard

PointGuard ($10 per species, per applicant) lets you surrender a drawn tag before the hunt for any reason. Your points are restored, plus the point you would have earned. PointGuard Plus ($25) covers all eligible big game species for three straight draw cycles. Neither is refundable, and you don't get the tag fee back.

Point creep and what "points to draw" means

Because of the bonus pass, the top hunts drift toward max-point holders. As more hunters buy points every year, the point total needed to draw in the bonus pass rises. That's point creep. Hunting media (not AZGFD) reported in 2025 that Kaibab late rifle mule deer took more than 27 points to draw; treat that as a rough estimate. The other 80% of tags still go by weighted random draw, so a low-point applicant always has some chance.

Worked example, elk (hypothetical numbers): A bull elk hunt has 50 tags. Up to 10 go in the bonus pass. Nonresidents can draw at most 5, and no more than 2 of those in the bonus pass. Say you're a nonresident with 6 elk points, a loyalty point and a hunter education point. That's 8 points, so you get 9 random numbers in each pass. If max-point holders sit well above you, you're counting on the random passes, where your 9 numbers beat a first-year applicant's 1 but still face long odds in a premium hunt.

Worked example, deer (hypothetical numbers): A Coues whitetail hunt has 300 tags. Nonresidents can draw up to 30, and up to 60 tags go in the bonus pass. With that many tags, many hunters draw with few or no points as a first or second choice. Remember that drawing resets your deer points, so don't burn a big point total on an easy hunt.

Strategy

  • Buying points for a premium hunt? Use the point-only number, or list only hunts you'd trade your points for.
  • Want to hunt now? List high-tag-count hunts first or second. Every point still adds a random number.
  • Keep applying every year to hold your loyalty point.
  • Get the hunter education point if you don't have it. For many nonresidents, Ethically Hunting Arizona is the way to earn it.
  • Hunt while you wait: Over-the-counter archery deer tags, nonpermit elk tags north of the Grand Canyon, and leftover tags in March (elk) and July (deer). Leftover tags don't touch your points.
  • Copper State Draw: In summer 2026 AZGFD added a separate Copper State Draw for a few extra deer, elk and turkey hunts. AZGFD says it doesn't affect your bonus points or your eligibility for the regular draws. Check whether it runs again.
  • Guided or private-land options: Arizona outfitters know unit-by-unit odds. Also see discount guided hunts and hunting leases.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Are Arizona bonus points the same as preference points? No. Points add random numbers and decide the 20% bonus pass, but the other tags are drawn randomly, so top point holders aren't guaranteed a tag.

Do my deer points work for both mule deer and Coues? Yes. Points are by genus, and both are deer.

Do I lose points if I draw my third choice? Yes. Any drawn elk or deer tag resets that genus to zero, whatever choice it was.

Can I build points without hunting? Yes. Use hunt number 3000 (elk) or 1000 (deer) and pay only the application fee plus a license.

title: California Preference Points Explained (Deer & Elk)
excerpt: How California's Big Game Drawing uses preference points for deer and elk: the 90/10 and 75/25 splits, point-only codes, fees, the one-nonresident elk rule, and how points are lost.
content:
California runs a preference point system with a random slice on top. For premium deer hunts, 90% of each hunt's tags go to the applicants with the most points and 10% are drawn at random. For elk (and pronghorn and bighorn sheep), 75% go by points and the rest at random once a hunt has four or more tags, and small hunts lean even harder on the random draw. In practice, if you want a top X zone deer tag or a bull elk tag, you either build points for many years or you put in every year and hope to hit the random pool.

California's deer system is also unusual in one helpful way: many deer zones don't need a draw at all. A, B and most D zone tags are sold until they run out, so you can build points and still hunt every year.

How you get points

You earn one point per species each year you apply in the Big Game Drawing and don't draw.

  • Deer: you earn a point when you don't draw your first-choice premium hunt, even if you draw your second or third choice.
  • Elk: you earn a point when you apply and don't draw an elk tag.
  • Point only, deer: buy a hunting license and a First Deer Tag Drawing Application and enter hunt code PD as your first choice. You can still list second and third choices to get a tag.
  • Point only, elk: buy the license and an elk drawing application and choose the elk preference-point-only code (listed as hunt 499 in CDFW's 2025 drawing statistics; confirm the current code in the digest before you apply).
  • Window: April 15 to midnight June 2 in 2026. No late applications.
  • License first: you need a current annual California hunting license. CDFW says the two-day nonresident license can't be used to apply for elk (or pronghorn), so nonresidents should plan on the annual license.
  • Age: at least 12 by July 1 (16 for bighorn sheep).

How points are used in the draw

Deer (premium hunts). 90% of each hunt's quota goes to first-choice applicants in order of points. The other 10% is a "draw-by-choice" random draw. A hunt with fewer than 10 tags gives one tag at random. Apprentice (junior) deer hunts split 50/50. You can list three choices; your points only count on the first. Second and third choices are filled in later rounds from whatever is left.

Elk. The split depends on the hunt's quota:

Many California elk hunts have only a handful of tags, so a big share of the state's elk tags go out at random.

Parties. A party's points are the plain average of its members' points, not rounded (8 points and 0 points = 4). Every member must list the same hunts in the same order. Deer parties aren't split when the party is bigger than the remaining tags; they're skipped. Elk parties can be split. Elk parties are limited to two, and nonresidents can't apply as a party for elk.

Residents vs. nonresidents

For deer, residents and nonresidents compete on equal terms. The deer application doubles as your tag purchase, so if you don't draw a premium hunt you can use it for an unrestricted zone. Nonresident refunds are limited, so read the digest's return rules.

For elk, the nonresident limit is the whole story. CDFW draws no more than one nonresident per license year for elk. A nonresident can build elk points, but the odds of drawing are tiny.

Keeping and losing points

  • Deer: you lose all deer points when you draw your first-choice premium hunt.
  • Elk: you lose all elk points when you receive an elk tag.
  • Five-year rule: you lose all points for a species if you don't take part in that species' drawing for five consecutive years. Moving out of state doesn't erase points.
  • Missed a year? You keep what you have but don't earn a point that year.
  • Point cap: 24 points is the most anyone can hold for any species in the 2026 drawing.
  • Returns: return an elk tag by mail before the season and you get a refund minus a $39.40 processing fee, and CDFW awards a point if the return is approved. Premium deer tags returned before the season can have points reinstated. Party members have extra limits.
  • Separate by species: deer and elk points never mix, and they can't be transferred.
  • Limits: one elk tag per license year; up to two deer tags but only one premium.

Point creep and what "points to draw" means

"Points to draw" is the lowest point level where a hunt's preference tags ran out last year. Each year more hunters stack up behind that line, so the number creeps up. With a 24-point cap, the top hunts have many applicants bunched near the maximum.

Deer example (based on 2025 statistics, our reading). In 2025, the X5B hunt had 45 preference tags, and by our count of CDFW's applicant table that quota ran out at about 19 points. CDFW doesn't publish a cutoff, so treat this as an estimate. Hunts like X12 cut off lower, and less popular premium hunts take far fewer points. Check CDFW's drawing statistics for your hunt. Hypothetically, if you have 6 points and want a hunt that took 19, the preference side is years away, so your real chance is the 10% random pool.

Elk example. 2025 bull hunts like Marble Mountains (34 tags, about 2,700 applicants) and Northeastern (15 tags, about 3,500 applicants) each had dozens of applicants at 16 points alone. Premium bull hunts are effectively a max-points game, with the random tags as the wildcard. Antlerless and either-sex hunts usually take far fewer points.

Strategy

  • Hunt deer every year while you build points. Put PD (or a long-shot premium hunt) first and an A, B or D zone second.
  • Apply for elk every year if you're a resident. Even if you never climb the point ladder, the random tags on small hunts are a real chance, and applying keeps the five-year clock from running out.
  • Nonresidents: elk is a lottery ticket. One nonresident a year. Spend your effort on deer, or on private-land elk.
  • Don't let points lapse. Apply at least once every five years for each species.
  • Private land changes the math. Ranches in CDFW's Private Lands Management (PLM) program issue their own deer and elk tags, and SHARE offers access hunts. Outfitters and hunting leases are the usual way in; check discount guided hunts too.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Do second and third deer choices cost me my point? No. You still earn a point if you miss your first choice, even when you draw a later choice.

Can I apply for elk as a nonresident? Yes, but only one nonresident is drawn each year for elk, and you can't apply in a party.

How do I lose points? Draw your first-choice premium deer hunt (deer) or receive a tag (elk), or skip the drawing for that species five years in a row.

Is there a nonresident deer quota? No. Nonresidents compete equally for deer tags.

Can I hunt deer without the draw? Yes. Unrestricted A, B and many D zone tags are sold until they fill.

title: Colorado Preference Points Explained (Elk & Deer)
excerpt: How Colorado's elk and deer preference points work for residents and nonresidents: earning points, the hybrid draw, nonresident caps, the 10-year rule, point creep, and 2026 key numbers.
content:
Colorado runs a preference point system with a small random "hybrid" draw on top. For elk and deer, the hunters with the most points get first crack at each hunt code, so the license goes to whoever has waited longest. A small share of licenses in the hardest hunts is drawn at random among applicants with five or more points. In practice, that means you can hunt many Colorado codes with zero to a few points, but the best trophy units take a decade or more. Elk and deer points are still free in 2026, so almost everyone who hunts Colorado builds them every year.

How you get points

You earn one point per species per year in the spring primary draw, in one of two ways:

  • Apply and miss your first choice. If your first-choice hunt code doesn't draw, you get a point for that species.
  • Apply for a point only. List the preference point code (P-999-99-P) as your first choice. You can't draw a license with it, but you get a point.

Either way, you need a few things first:

  • A qualifying license. You must own a current-year qualifying license before you can apply. The cheapest for most people is the annual small game license: $38.49 for residents and $104.86 for nonresidents (adult, 2026). A spring turkey license also qualifies ($38.49 resident, $194.21 nonresident). You can buy it in the same checkout, as long as it goes in your cart first.
  • The Habitat Stamp ($12.76, ages 18 to 64) on your first purchase of the year.
  • The application fee: $8.93 per species for residents and $11.49 for nonresidents. It is nonrefundable. There is no separate point fee for elk or deer.
  • Age: You must be 12 to hunt big game. An 11-year-old can apply for a point if they turn 12 by the end of the year.

The secondary draw, leftovers, and over-the-counter (OTC) tags neither use nor award points.

How points are used in the draw

Only your first choice uses points. You can list four choices per species. CPW fills first choices in order of points, highest first. Second through fourth choices are drawn afterward and don't use points.

Drawing your first choice resets that species to zero. Drawing a later choice leaves your points alone.

The hybrid draw. For the toughest hunts, CPW holds back a share of licenses for a random draw:

  • The hunt code must have taken 10 or more resident points to draw the year before and have at least five licenses.
  • You need at least five points, must apply on your own (no groups), and must list the hybrid code as your first choice.
  • CPW has described the hybrid draw as covering up to 20% of the licenses in those codes.
  • If you win, you lose all your points for that species. If you miss, you get a point.

Hunters sometimes confuse this with the six-point line. That number is for the nonresident cap, not the hybrid draw.

Nonresident caps. Nonresidents compete in the same draw as residents but can take only a share of each hunt code:

  • Hunt codes that took six or more points for an adult resident: up to 20% to nonresidents.
  • Hunt codes that took fewer than six points: up to 25% to nonresidents (this was 35% in earlier years).
  • CPW sets each code's category from the average of the three most recent limited draws, with a one-year lag. For 2026 it used the 2022 to 2024 draws.
  • The cap can loosen if licenses are left after all resident first choices are drawn. Caps don't apply in the secondary draw or to leftovers.

Group applications. Elk and deer groups can be any size. Everyone lists the same hunt codes in the same order, and the group is drawn at the point level of its lowest member. If one person makes an error, the whole group is disqualified. A mixed resident and nonresident group gets nothing if the nonresident cap is already full. Groups can't apply for hybrid codes.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Residents and nonresidents earn points the same way and use the same point pool for each species.

Keeping and losing points

  • Drawing your first choice resets that species to zero (including a hybrid win).
  • The 10-year rule. You lose your points for a species if you go 10 consecutive years without applying for or holding a license for it. Applying for a point-only code counts as applying, so one point application a decade keeps you active.
  • Surrendering a license. If you draw and can't go, surrendering by the posted deadline (June 1 in 2026) gets your points restored. Later returns get a refund or points back, not both.
  • No waiting period for elk or deer. You can apply again the next year.
  • Separate by species. Elk points and deer points are tracked separately and can't be swapped. They aren't tied to a unit, so you can use them anywhere in the state.

Point creep and "points to draw"

CPW's draw recaps show the lowest point level at which someone drew each hunt code. That's "points to draw": last year's floor, not a promise. Because more people build points each year than there are licenses, many codes need a little more every year. That's point creep.

Elk example (hypothetical). Say a rifle bull code took 6 points last year. With 6 points you're on the line, since some at that level drew and some didn't. With 7 you're likely in. With 4 you have no chance in the preference draw, so hunt OTC or a leftover cow tag and apply again.

Deer example. CPW reported that a GMU 512 buck license took 11 resident and 12 nonresident points in the 2024 draw. A nonresident with 9 points is two or three years out, or more with point creep.

Rough tiers (elk and deer):

These tiers are our rough estimates from recent draw results and hunting-media summaries, not CPW figures. Always check CPW's draw recap for the exact code you want.

Strategy

  • Always get your point. Points are free beyond the application fee, so apply every year.
  • Use your second choices. List codes that had leftovers in past years so you still hunt without spending points.
  • Hunt OTC while you wait. Colorado still sells OTC elk licenses in many units. Nonresident archery elk west of I-25 and in GMU 140 has moved to a limited draw, but nonresident OTC rifle options remain. See OTC elk tags.
  • Landowner vouchers. Some outfitters hunt private land with landowner preference vouchers, which skip the point line. See our hunting leases and discount guided hunts.
  • Plan for 2028. Starting with the 2028 draw, CPW will split each hunt code 50/50 between a preference draw and a bonus draw, give nonresidents a flat 25% share, drop the point-only code, and add a point fee (amount not yet final). CPW's adopted summary doesn't spell out exactly how banked elk and deer points will be applied, so watch for its guidance. The 2027 draw runs under the current rules.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Do I have to buy a license to get a point? Yes. You need a current-year qualifying license, such as small game, before you can apply, even for a point only.

Can I get elk and deer points in the same year? Yes. Each species has its own application and its own points.

Will my points still count after the 2028 changes? CPW hasn't published the full details yet. Its adopted summary doesn't say exactly how banked elk and deer points will be used in the new split draw, so keep building them and check CPW's updates before 2028.

title: Preference & Bonus Points by State (Western Elk and Deer)
excerpt: How every western state draws elk and deer tags, side by side: preference vs. bonus points, what a point costs, nonresident quotas, and how you lose points.
content:
Every western state hands out its best elk and deer tags through a draw, but no two states run that draw the same way. Some reward the people who have waited longest. Some only improve your odds a little each year. A few ignore points entirely. Knowing which system you're dealing with is the difference between a smart ten-year plan and a decade of wasted application fees.

This page puts all eleven western states plus Alaska side by side. Each state also has its own detailed page (linked in the table), and you can check real unit-by-unit odds with our draw odds tool.

Draw odds

Check your odds for any unit

Pick a state, species and your points to see last year's results for every hunt.

Open the odds tool

The four kinds of draw

Preference points. The applicants with the most points draw first. If a hunt took 8 points last year and you have 8, you're in good shape. It's predictable, but the best hunts can take decades, and "point creep" pushes the line higher every year. Colorado, Wyoming (nonresidents), Oregon, California and Montana's nonresident combination licenses work this way, usually with a slice of tags held back for a random draw.

Bonus points. Points buy you extra chances in a random draw instead of a place in line. You can draw with zero points, and you can miss with twenty. Arizona and Utah give one extra entry per point and reserve part of the tags for the top point holders.

Squared bonus points. Your points are squared, so the advantage grows quickly the longer you apply. Nevada, Montana's permits and B licenses, and Washington's special permits use squared points. Everything is random; nothing is reserved for max-point holders.

No points. Idaho, New Mexico and Alaska draw purely at random. Your odds are the same in year one as in year ten, so there's no reason to "build" anything. Just apply where the odds are best.

State by state

Fees are for the 2026 draw and change often. Use them to compare states, then confirm in each state's current regulations before you apply.

How to use this

Build points in two or three preference states. Colorado's points are free in 2026, and Wyoming and Oregon points let you plan years ahead. Pick hunts you can realistically draw within your planning horizon.

Add one or two bonus states as long shots. Arizona, Utah, Nevada and Montana permits can pay off any year, and your odds improve every time you apply. Squared states reward sticking with it.

Apply every year in no-point states. Idaho, New Mexico and Alaska cost little to enter and give everyone the same shot, so they're your best chance at a tag this season.

Don't forget hunts that don't need points. Over-the-counter and general tags, leftover lists, landowner tags and private-land hunts can put you in the field while your points grow. Our state guides cover these, and outfitters in our directory often hold landowner or private-land tags.

title: Idaho Controlled Hunt Draw Explained (Elk & Deer): No Points, Pure Luck
excerpt: Idaho has no preference or bonus points. Here's how the random controlled hunt draw, the 10% nonresident limit, the one-year wait after drawing a bull or buck hunt, and the new nonresident general tag drawing work for elk and deer.
content:
Idaho is one of the few western states with no points of any kind. There are no preference points, no bonus points, and nothing to buy to "build" toward a hunt. Every application gets one random draw number, and a first-year applicant has exactly the same chance as someone who has applied for 20 years. That is good news if you want a shot at a quality hunt without a decade-long wait. The tradeoff is that you can't plan around a point total. Your odds in a tough hunt stay low every year, and patience earns you nothing.

Idaho actually runs two separate drawings for deer and elk:

  • Controlled hunts (May–June). Limited-entry hunts with set tag numbers, open to residents and nonresidents.
  • The nonresident general tag drawing (December). New since the 2026 season. Nonresidents now draw for general season deer and elk tags instead of buying them first come, first served.

How you "get points" in Idaho

You don't. Idaho has no point system and no point-only purchase. Not drawing this year gives you no advantage next year, and skipping a year costs you nothing.

What you do need before you apply for either drawing is a current Idaho hunting license. A nonresident adult license is $185 (it includes a three-day fishing license), plus a $10 access/depredation fee charged once a year. Residents pay $15.75 plus a $5 fee. The license is not refunded if you don't draw. Hunters born after 1974 must have hunter education on file with Idaho Fish and Game (IDFG).

How the controlled hunt draw works

Controlled hunts are applied for May 1 – June 5 (2026 dates). Each application lists a first choice and an optional second choice by four-digit hunt number. Applications that miss on their first choice go into the second-choice drawing, but only if that second-choice hunt still has tags. In practice, popular hunts fill on first choices, so use your second choice on a hunt with better odds.

  • Groups: two to four hunters can apply together for deer, elk, or pronghorn. Everyone must list the same hunts. If a group is larger than the tags left in a hunt, it isn't drawn for that hunt.
  • Fees: the application fee is $18 for nonresidents and $6.25 for residents, nonrefundable. If you draw, you buy the tag by August 1.
  • Second drawing: tags not applied for, and tags not bought by August 1, go into a second drawing (August 5–15 in 2026). Anything left after that is sold first come, first served.

The 10% nonresident limit

In the first controlled hunt drawing, Idaho's long-standing rule is that nonresidents can draw no more than 10% of the tags in a hunt, and no more than 10% of the tags for the species. Some hunts list their own nonresident tag limit in the controlled hunt tables, so check the current Big Game Seasons and Rules for the hunt you want. In hunts with 10 or fewer tags, no more than one tag can go to a nonresident. This is a cap, not a guarantee. Because the draw is random, nonresidents may get fewer than 10% in some hunts.

Two exceptions: the 10% limit doesn't apply to unlimited hunts or to tags sold or drawn after the first drawing. And if a resident applies in a group with a nonresident, IDFG treats the whole application as a nonresident application.

The one-year wait after drawing a bull or buck hunt

Idaho's rule is the closest thing it has to a points penalty. If you draw an antlered-only controlled deer or elk hunt (or a pronghorn hunt), you can't apply for any controlled hunt for that species the following year. The exceptions are the second application period, unlimited hunts, and Landowner Appreciation Program hunts. Antlerless and either-sex hunts don't trigger the wait.

How the nonresident general tag drawing works

Nonresidents who want a general season tag now apply December 5–15, 2026 for the 2027 season, with a second round February 5–15, 2027. Each application can list up to five choices. For elk, a choice is a zone and an A or B tag. For deer, it's a unit and either a regular or white-tailed deer tag.

IDFG gives every application a random number and issues tags from lowest to highest number. All first choices are processed first, then all second choices, and so on through the fifth. Groups of up to four count as one application with one number, and a group only draws if there are tags for everyone. The application fee is $18 per species. If you draw a species in round one, you can't apply for it in round two, even if you don't buy the tag.

The statewide nonresident general quota is 12,815 elk tags and 15,500 deer tags (regular and white-tailed combined), including tags allocated to outfitters. Residents don't draw for general tags. They buy them over the counter, and capped elk zones have their own resident sales. Holding a general tag from this drawing does not stop you from applying for controlled hunts.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Keeping and losing points

There are no points to keep or lose. The only things to track are the one-year wait above, which is triggered by drawing (not by filling your tag), and the limit of one application per species in each drawing. Deer and elk are handled separately.

"Point creep" and what odds really mean here

Point creep can't happen in Idaho, because nobody is stacking points. What changes from year to year is the number of applicants. Your odds in a hunt are roughly the number of tags available to your residency group divided by the number of first-choice applicants. IDFG posts the previous year's drawing odds for each hunt in its Hunt Planner, and says controlled hunt odds range from 100% to under 5%.

Worked example, elk (hypothetical numbers): Say a premium controlled bull hunt has 50 tags. Nonresidents can draw at most 5 (10%). If 400 nonresidents apply, each has roughly a 1-in-80 chance, every year, no matter how long they've applied. Over 10 years of applying, that adds up to only about a 12% chance (roughly 1 in 8) of ever drawing. Compare that with the 2026 nonresident general elk drawing, where IDFG drew 32% of all elk applicants. Some zones, such as Lolo and Selway A, drew every first-choice applicant, while capped zones like Diamond Creek B and South Hills B drew about 4%.

Worked example, deer (from IDFG's 2026 draw data): In the 2026 nonresident general deer drawing, IDFG drew 54% of applicants. Many regular deer units drew every first-choice applicant, while the toughest drew under 9%. List a hard unit first and an easy one second, and you still have a real chance at a tag.

Strategy

  • Apply every year for the hunt you really want. Once you have a license, it costs only the application fee, and missing carries no penalty.
  • Use your other choices. In the general drawing, list at least one zone or unit that drew 100% last year. In the controlled draw, make your second choice a hunt with good odds.
  • Mind the one-year wait. Drawing a so-so antlered-only hunt locks you out of controlled hunts for that species next year.
  • Consider antlerless hunts. IDFG offers many, and they don't trigger the wait.
  • Talk to outfitters. Some hold outfitter-allocated general tags for booked clients. Also see discount guided hunts and hunting leases.
  • Watch the returned tag sales. IDFG sells returned and leftover tags over the counter several times a year.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Can I buy a point in Idaho? No. Idaho has no preference or bonus points and no point-only option.

Do nonresidents still get over-the-counter general tags? Not at first. Since the 2026 season, nonresident general deer and elk tags are drawn in December. Unclaimed and returned tags are later sold over the counter.

If I draw a cow elk controlled hunt, do I have to sit out a year? No. The one-year wait applies to antlered-only deer and elk hunts (and pronghorn), not to antlerless hunts.

Does applying with a resident friend help a nonresident? No. IDFG treats a mixed group as a nonresident application in the controlled hunt draw.

title: Montana Bonus Points Explained (Elk & Deer)
excerpt: How Montana's two point systems work for elk and deer: squared bonus points for permits and B licenses, nonresident combination license preference points (3-point cap), fees, purchase windows, and 2026 key numbers.
content:
Montana runs two separate point systems, and most confusion comes from mixing them up. Bonus points apply to limited draws such as elk and deer permits and B licenses. They are squared, so each point adds more entries, but every draw is still random. Preference points apply only to the nonresident combination licenses that carry a general elk and/or deer license. Those are a short line capped at three points, plus a random pool for people with none. For a nonresident, the combination license gets you in the door. A permit, if you want one, is a squared-odds lottery on top.

How you get points

Bonus points (residents and nonresidents) - At application: Answer "yes" to the bonus point question on each permit or license application. It costs $2 for residents and $20 for nonresidents per license or permit. - Point only: If you didn't apply for that license type, buy a point from July 1 to September 30 for $15 (resident) or $25 (nonresident). - Limit: One bonus point per license type per year. - Age: You must be old enough to apply for that license or permit.

Preference points (nonresidents only, combination licenses) - At application: Add a point for $100 when you apply for a Big Game, Elk, or Deer Combination. - Point only: If you aren't applying, buy one for $100 from July 1 to December 31. - Outfitter point: Clients of a Montana-licensed outfitter can buy a second $100 point at application. A license drawn with it is valid only while hunting with an outfitter. - Cap: No one can hold more than three preference points.

Prerequisites. Nonresidents need the conservation license ($10) and base hunting license ($50) when they apply, plus the $7.50 Aquatic Invasive Species Prevention Pass at 16 and older. Residents need the conservation license ($8) and base hunting license ($10). Nonresidents must hold, or apply for, the right combination license before they can apply for a deer or elk permit.

How points are used in the draw

Bonus points: squared. Your accumulated points, including the one you buy this year, are squared, then you get one more entry for the application itself. With 3 points you have 3² + 1 = 10 chances. With 10 points you have 101. It's still a random draw, so a zero-point applicant can win and a high-point applicant can lose.

Two rules catch people: - Points count only for your first choice. - You have to buy a point that year for your points to count. If you apply without electing a bonus point, your saved points aren't used in that drawing. They aren't lost, though.

Preference points: 75/25. For nonresident combination licenses: - 75% go to applicants in order of most preference points. - 25% go by random draw to applicants who hold no preference points.

With the three-point cap, the line can never be more than three years long. Usually it's shorter.

Nonresident permit cap. By state law, nonresidents are limited to (but not guaranteed) 10% of an elk or deer permit quota.

Parties. Two to five people can apply together. Everyone must choose the same license and the same point participation. Bonus points are averaged and rounded to the nearest whole number. Preference points are averaged to three decimals. A party gets one entry, so applying together doesn't improve your odds.

Landowner preference. Up to 15% of many permit and B license quotas are set aside for qualifying landowners (and family, employees, or designees). Landowner rules for nonresident combination licenses have been changing, so check the current regulations if that applies to you.

How permits and general licenses fit together

  • A general license (residents buy elk for $20 and deer for $16 over the counter; nonresidents get one through a combination) lets you hunt general districts.
  • A permit is not a second animal. It restricts your general license to a specific district or season, such as many mule deer buck or trophy elk districts. Residents buy the general license and apply for the permit. Nonresidents apply for a combination and the permit together by April 1.
  • B licenses (Elk B, Deer B) are extra antlerless licenses with their own draws and their own bonus points. The deadline is June 1.
  • Elk permit refund option. If you apply for both and draw the combination license but not the elk permit, FWP has offered an option to return the combination for an 80% refund. Your preference points go to zero.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Keeping and losing points

Bonus points - Deleted when you draw your first choice in a year you elected a bonus point. - Deleted if you lose hunting privileges by court action. - No rule deletes them for skipping years. They just sit unused until you buy a point and apply again. - Kept separately by species and license type (elk permit, Deer B, and so on).

Preference points - Deleted when you draw a combination license, even if you return it later. - Deleted if you hold points and skip the next combination drawing.

There's no waiting period after drawing elk or deer.

Point creep and "points to draw"

With bonus points there's no point level that guarantees a tag. "Points to draw" really means "points where my odds get decent." Each point helps more than the last, but the people at the top of the pool also gain every year. On some top permits, odds stay in the single digits even at high points, especially for nonresidents limited to 10%.

Elk example (hypothetical). Two hunters apply for the same elk permit. One has 0 points and buys one (1² + 1 = 2 chances). The other has 5 saved plus this year's (6² + 1 = 37 chances). The second has about 18 times as many entries, but both are still in a lottery.

Deer example (hypothetical). A nonresident wants a mule deer buck permit. Year one: they draw the Deer Combination and miss the permit, earning a bonus point. Year three, with 3 points: 10 chances. Their combination license is still good for a general district if the permit doesn't come through.

Combination licenses. Under the 75/25 rule with a three-point cap, combination licenses usually go to applicants with one to three points or to the zero-point random pool. Results shift every year with demand.

Strategy

  • Buy a bonus point every year you apply. If you skip the point, your saved points don't count that year.
  • Don't apply for a combo with points "just to see." Drawing wipes your preference points even if you return the license.
  • Points-only years: Buy a preference point by December 31 and bonus points by September 30.
  • Zero points isn't hopeless. A quarter of combination licenses go only to people with no points.
  • General districts are the fallback. A combination license or a resident general license works across general districts without a permit. Block Management opens private land at no cost.
  • Outfitters. The outfitter preference point can help a guided hunter draw. Outfitters with private leases can also make a general license a good hunt. See hunting leases and discount guided hunts.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Are preference points still around for 2026? Yes. The 2026 regulations keep $100 nonresident preference points for combination licenses, the 75/25 split, the three-point cap, and the outfitter point.

Do I lose bonus points if I skip a year? No, but they only count in a year you buy a bonus point.

Do residents get preference points? No. Residents buy general licenses over the counter and use bonus points for permits and B licenses.

Do elk points help with deer? No. Points are tracked by species and license type.

title: Nevada Bonus Points Explained (Mule Deer & Elk)
excerpt: How Nevada's squared bonus point draw works for mule deer and elk: earning points, point-only applications, the five-choice draw, the nonresident guided deer draw, elk waiting periods, fees and quotas.
content:
Nevada uses a squared bonus point system, and it is a true lottery. No tags are set aside for top point holders. Every application gets one random draw number, plus extra numbers equal to your bonus points squared. The lowest number wins. Points make a big difference as they stack up, since 5 points gives you 26 numbers instead of 1. But a first-year applicant can still draw a great tag, and a 15-point applicant can still miss. Nevada sells no over-the-counter mule deer or elk tags, so this system decides almost every hunt.

How you get points

  • Apply and don't draw. You earn one point per hunt category for each unsuccessful application, as long as you hold an active Nevada hunting license.
  • Buy a point only. A bonus point only application costs $10. It's exempt from the $3 game tag application fee and the $5 elk fee. You can buy points during the main application period or the second draw period in June, when bonus points for all big game species go on sale.
  • License required. You must hold a hunting license for that license year to earn a point. Nevada lets you apply and buy the license only if you draw, but that application earns no point.
  • One point per year. You can earn only one point per category per license year.
  • No points while waiting. You can't buy bonus points for a category while you're in a waiting period for it.

Licenses for 2026 are $38 (resident adult hunting), $75 (resident adult combination) and $155 (nonresident adult combination). Youth 12–17 pay $15. You must be 12 to hunt big game, and a parent or guardian signs for applicants under 18.

How points are used in the draw

The squared formula. Every application gets one random number between 1 and 100 million. If you have bonus points, you get more numbers: your points squared, plus one for the current year. The draw uses your lowest number.

Five choices. You can list up to five unit-and-season choices per species and sex class, as long as five different hunts are available. NDOW recommends using all five. If your first choice fills before your number comes up, your later choices still give you a shot.

Separate categories. Antlered mule deer, antlered elk, antlerless elk and spike elk each have their own bonus points. You can apply for spike elk while you build antlered elk points.

Quotas. Commission Policy 24 sets tags at about 90% resident and 10% nonresident. In many small unit groups, that leaves one or two nonresident tags.

Party applications. A party has at least two hunters who apply for the same hunts. The party's points are averaged and rounded to the nearest whole number, and the party draws together or not at all.

The nonresident guided mule deer draw

Nonresidents can apply in a separate guided mule deer draw. In 2026 it ran February 9 to March 9, with results March 20. A licensed Nevada master guide or subguide must sign your application and stay with you in the field. Immediate family of the guide can't apply. The guided quota is a percentage of the nonresident tags issued the year before, so the odds can be better than the regular nonresident pool. The tradeoff is the guide's fee. Check NDOW's current fee table for the guided tag price, since the 2026 regulations' fee table doesn't list it separately.

Nevada has no guided draw for elk.

Residents vs. nonresidents

The draw itself works the same way for both groups.

Keeping and losing points

  • Drawing resets you. Your points in a category go to zero when you draw or buy a tag in that category.
  • Don't skip two years. You forfeit your points if you fail to apply in a category for two consecutive years, when a season for that category was offered. A bonus point only application is an application in that category, so buying a point each year should keep you active. Confirm in the current regulations.
  • Elk waiting periods. If you draw an antlered elk tag, you may not apply for antlered elk for the next 7 open seasons, whether or not you kill a bull. Antlerless and spike elk have no waiting period. Mule deer has no waiting period in the 2026 rules.
  • Report your harvest. A missed harvest report can cost you a year of big game tags.

Point creep and "points to draw"

In a squared system, "points to draw" doesn't mean a cutoff. It means the point level where your odds become reasonable. As more hunters pile up points, your odds at any given level slowly fall.

Mule deer example: Say a unit group has 10 nonresident tags and 300 applicants. A 0-point applicant holds 1 number. A 6-point applicant holds 37 numbers. If most of the field sits at 2–4 points, the 6-pointer has noticeably better odds but is still far from a sure thing.

Elk example: Antlered elk tags are scarce, and drawing one starts a 7-season wait. A 10-point applicant holds 101 numbers against a 2-point applicant's 5. That's about 20 times as many chances, but on a unit with only a few nonresident bull tags, both may still miss for years.

Strategy

  • Apply every year. The two-year rule is the easiest way to lose a big point total. If you won't hunt, buy the $10 point.
  • Use all five choices. List the hunt you want first and a higher-odds hunt farther down. Drawing any choice resets your points, so only list hunts you'd be glad to hunt.
  • Spike and antlerless elk. They have separate points and no waiting period, which makes them a good way to hunt elk while you build antlered points.
  • Nonresidents: Weigh the guided draw if you plan to hire an outfitter anyway. Specialty Silver State and Dream tag drawings are another long shot.
  • Outfitters and private land: See discount guided hunts and hunting leases.

Draw odds

Check your Nevada odds

Pick Nevada, a species and your bonus points to see what your chances look like.

Open the odds tool

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Are bonus points or preference points better? Nevada's squared bonus points never guarantee a tag. The upside is that anyone can draw in any year.

Do my deer points help me draw elk? No. Each category has its own points, and antlered, antlerless and spike elk are all separate.

Do I need to buy a license to get a point? Yes. You need a hunting license for that year.

What if I draw an antlered elk tag and don't hunt? The 7-season wait still applies, and your antlered elk points reset.

title: New Mexico Draw Explained (Elk & Deer): No Points, Three Pools
excerpt: New Mexico has no preference or bonus points. Here's how the random elk and deer draw, the 84/10/6 resident, outfitter and nonresident pools, landowner (EPLUS) tags, and leftover licenses work.
content:
New Mexico runs a pure random draw with no points. The state says plainly that it does not give preference to applicants who were unsuccessful in earlier drawings. Every application gets a random place in line, and a first-time applicant has the same chance as someone who has applied for 20 years. That makes New Mexico a favorite for nonresidents who don't want to wait a decade. The catch is the pool system: by law, at least 84% of draw licenses go to residents, so nonresident odds in the best elk and deer units are low every year.

How you "get points" in New Mexico

You don't. There are no preference points, no bonus points, and no point-only purchase. Missing the draw doesn't help you next year, and skipping a year doesn't hurt you.

What you do need before you apply:

  • A current game-hunting license: $25 resident, $90 nonresident (2026–27). It is not refunded if you don't draw.
  • A Habitat Management and Access Validation (HMAV), $4, for hunters 18 and older, and a Habitat Stamp, $10, if you'll hunt Forest Service or BLM land.
  • Last season's harvest reports. If you held a deer or elk license last season, you must report even if you didn't hunt. Miss the final deadline (March 18 in 2026) and all of your draw applications are rejected.

How the draw works

Your place in line is random

After the deadline (March 18, 2026, 5 p.m. MDT), every application is randomly assigned a sequence number. The computer then works down the list one application at a time. For each one, it tries your first choice, then your second, then your third, before moving on to the next applicant. If all three are full, you get nothing and it moves on.

That means your second and third choices matter a lot. A lucky sequence number can land your third choice before an unlucky applicant's first choice is ever looked at.

The three pools

Every hunt's licenses are split three ways under state law:

A license is issued only if there is room in your pool for that hunt. Fractions round to the nearest whole license, so small hunts may have no license at all in the 6% pool. If one pool doesn't fill, the leftover licenses can be moved to another category, with residents offered undersubscribed hunts first when practicable.

The outfitter pool: To apply in it, you need a signed contract with a registered New Mexico outfitter before you apply, and you list the outfitter's registration number on your application. If you draw, that outfitter must guide you for at least two days in the hunt area. Nonresidents who apply in the 6% pool can still hire an outfitter after they draw.

Mixed groups: Up to four people can apply on one application (one applicant plus three who attach). A resident applying with a nonresident gets licenses only if both the resident and nonresident pools have room.

The fourth choice

For deer and elk you can add a fourth choice: a quadrant of the state. After all applications are examined, a second pass hands leftover licenses to applicants who listed a fourth choice. You'll get the same weapon type as your first choice, but it could be any hunt in that quadrant, and an elk applicant could end up with an antlerless hunt. There are no refunds for a fourth-choice draw. Only use it if you'd happily take any license.

What nonresidents can apply for

Nonresidents can apply for mature bull and either-sex elk hunts. Antlerless elk hunts and hunts held only on state wildlife management areas are residents only.

You pay up front

When you apply, your card is charged the full license fee, which includes a nonrefundable application fee ($7 resident, $13 nonresident). If you don't draw, the license fee is refunded, but the application fee, game-hunting license, and stamps are not.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Keeping and losing points

There are no points to keep or lose, and no waiting period after you draw deer or elk. The rules that can still knock you out:

  • Harvest reports. No report by the deadline means every draw application that year is rejected.
  • One license per species. You can't hold more than one license for the same big game species in a license year unless a rule allows it.
  • Elk: draw or private land, not both. You can't hold a private-land elk license and a draw elk license in the same license year.

Point creep and what odds really mean here

Without points, there's no point creep. Your odds are simply the licenses in your pool divided by the applicants competing for them. The department suggests estimating it this way: multiply a hunt's total licenses by your pool's share (0.84, 0.10 or 0.06), then compare that with how many applicants in your pool drew last year in its draw odds reports.

Worked example, elk (hypothetical numbers): A bull elk hunt has 100 licenses. About 84 go to residents, 10 to the outfitter pool, and 6 to nonresidents without an outfitter. If 600 nonresidents list it first, each has roughly a 1% chance, and the same 1% next year. Odds can look better in the outfitter pool, but that pool is shared with residents and varies hunt to hunt.

Worked example, deer (hypothetical numbers): A deer hunt has 50 licenses. The nonresident pool gets 3, the outfitter pool 5. In a hunt that small, a nonresident's chance depends almost entirely on how many others apply. A less popular unit with 300 licenses gives 18 nonresident licenses, which is why many hunters put a solid backup hunt in their second or third slot.

Strategy

  • Apply every year. There's no penalty for missing, and luck is the whole game.
  • Don't fill all three choices with prime units. The department itself warns that three premium choices make your overall odds poor. Put a realistic hunt second or third.
  • Look at bow and muzzleloader hunts. They draw fewer applicants, though success rates are often lower.
  • Residents: consider cow elk. Antlerless hunts generally get far fewer applications than bull hunts.
  • Use the outfitter pool if you were going to book a guide anyway.
  • Look at private-land elk. Under EPLUS, landowners receive elk authorizations. A unit-wide authorization lets you hunt public land and unit-wide ranches in that unit, while a ranch-only authorization is good only on that ranch. In secondary-zone units, private-land licenses are sold over the counter with a landowner's ranch code. An authorization is not a license; you still buy the license from the department. See how private-land elk tags work, or browse hunting leases and discount guided hunts.
  • Private-land deer: Some deer licenses in units 2A, 2B, 2C, 4 and 5A are private-land only and are drawn on the same application. You need a landowner authorization number to hunt them.
  • Leftovers: Unclaimed licenses go on sale in summer, first come, first served, with residents getting the first 24 hours. In 2026 the July 8 sale was deer only.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Can I buy points in New Mexico? No. There are no points and no point-only option.

Does the outfitter pool guarantee better odds? No. It's a separate 10% share, open to residents and nonresidents with an outfitter contract. Odds vary by hunt, so check the department's draw reports.

Can a nonresident draw a cow elk tag? Not in the draw. Antlerless elk draw hunts are residents only. Private-land elk licenses are another route.

What if I miss my harvest report? All of your draw applications for the year are rejected.

title: Oregon Preference Points Explained (Elk & Deer)
excerpt: How Oregon's controlled hunt preference points work for elk and deer: the 75/25 split, first-choice-only points, the point saver, the 5% nonresident cap, party averaging, fees, and what it takes to draw.
content:
Oregon uses a modified preference point system for controlled deer and elk hunts. In each hunt, 75% of the tags go to first-choice applicants in order of points, most points first. The other 25% are drawn at random among all first-choice applicants, whatever their points. For you, that means points are a place in line for most tags, plus a small lottery that gives a 0-point hunter a real, if slim, chance. Two rules shape every Oregon plan: points only work on your first choice, and nonresidents can get no more than 5% of the tags in any controlled deer or elk hunt.

How you get points

  • Apply and don't draw your first choice. You earn one point in that hunt series. Buck deer is the 100 series and elk is the 200 series. You can earn only one point per series per year.
  • Draw a lower choice and you still get a point. If you miss your first choice but draw your second through fifth, your points still go up by one.
  • Point Saver. If you don't want to hunt a controlled hunt in that series, buy a Point Saver instead. You get a point and keep your existing points. ODFW sells it from December 1 to May 15 and again from July 1 to November 30, online or from license agents. You can't list other hunt choices in that series the same year.
  • License first. You must buy an Oregon annual hunting license before you apply or buy a Point Saver: $39 for residents and $193 for nonresidents in 2026.
  • Age. Youth can build points starting at age 9. A youth who buys a Point Saver can't apply for a First Time Youth tag in that series the same year.
  • Missed the deadline? If you didn't apply in the May drawing, you can still buy a point for that series from July 1 through November 30.

A Point Saver doesn't stop you from hunting general seasons. A general-season tag is a separate purchase that doesn't affect your controlled hunt points.

How points are used in the draw

  1. First choices with points. For each hunt, 75% of the tags go to first-choice applicants, highest points first.
  2. First choices at random. The remaining 25% are drawn at random among all first-choice applicants who didn't draw in step 1. Points don't help here.
  3. Second through fifth choices. Any tags still left go to later choices by random draw, ignoring points.

You can list up to five choices per series on one application. The 2026 application deadline was May 15, with online changes allowed through May 25 and results by June 12.

Nonresident cap. Nonresidents can receive up to 5% of the tags in each controlled deer and elk hunt. In a 40-tag hunt, that's two tags at most. In hunts with fewer than 35 tags, the rule allows one nonresident tag. Nothing in ODFW's 2027 proposals changes the cap.

Party applications. Deer and elk parties have no size limit. Everyone's points are totaled and averaged. An average of .51 or higher rounds up, and .50 or lower rounds down. The leader's choices apply to everyone, and the party draws together or not at all.

Premium hunts are separate. They're drawn purely at random with no points, and parties aren't allowed.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Oregon's rule sets the application fee at $8 plus a $2 license agent fee for 2026–27. It goes up to $9 plus $2 in 2028–29.

Keeping and losing points

  • Drawing your first choice resets you to zero, even if you never buy the tag. Pioneer license holders and resident disabled veterans 65 and older reset to one point.
  • Skipping years doesn't cost you. Oregon rules say you don't forfeit points for not applying. Points stay in the system until you draw your first choice.
  • License suspension does. If your license is suspended or revoked, you forfeit all your points.
  • No waiting periods for deer or elk after you draw.
  • Separate series. Buck deer (100), elk (200), pronghorn (400), antlerless deer (600) and spring bear (700) points are all separate. Points belong to the series, not a hunt number, so you can switch hunts each year.

2026 deer change: Eastern Oregon buck hunts moved to new deer hunt areas with new hunt codes. Your 100 series points carried over unchanged.

Point creep and "points to draw"

"Points to draw" is the lowest point level where the 75% pool ran out last year. In ODFW's 2026 draw reports, a deer and an elk example show how far apart hunts can be:

Elk: Heppner No. 1 (248A1) took about 5 points for residents to be near-certain and about 6 for nonresidents. Ochoco No. 1 (237X) took 9 to 11 resident points, and nonresidents drew only here and there in the teens and 20s. Some big-tag hunts took 0 points.

Deer: Deschutes 01 Bow and Fox 01 Bow drew everyone who applied, residents and nonresidents. Crooked River 01 rifle drew nearly every resident with 2 or more points. Trout Creek 01 needed around 20 resident points, and only 2 of 443 nonresidents drew.

Point creep happens when more people sit at the top point levels than there are 75%-pool tags. The cutoff then rises a little each year. For nonresidents, the 5% cap makes it worse, since a small hunt may have just one nonresident tag.

Strategy

  • Put your dream hunt first only if you're building points for it. Otherwise, use your first choice on a hunt you can draw now, and save points for later.
  • Use choices two to five on hunts that had leftover tags. They don't cost points.
  • Buy a Point Saver in years you can't hunt. Drawing a first choice you won't use wipes out your points.
  • Hunt general seasons while you wait. Western Oregon blacktail and many archery elk hunts are over the counter. See general season elk tags and general season deer tags.
  • Nonresidents: With a 5% cap, private-land hunts through outfitters are often the realistic route for eastern Oregon bulls and mule deer. See hunting leases and discount guided hunts.

Are deer and elk points shared? No. Each series keeps its own points.

title: Utah Bonus and Preference Points Explained (Elk & Deer)
excerpt: How Utah's two point systems work for elk and deer: bonus points for limited-entry and once-in-a-lifetime hunts, preference points for general-season deer, point-only applications, waiting periods, fees and nonresident permits.
content:
Utah runs two point systems side by side. Bonus points cover limited-entry hunts (including premium limited-entry deer and limited-entry bull elk) and once-in-a-lifetime species. Half of each hunt's permits go to the applicants with the most bonus points, and the other half are drawn at random, with extra chances for every point you hold. Preference points cover general-season buck deer, and that draw is straight seniority: the most points draw first. In practice, a bonus point never guarantees a limited-entry permit, but it always helps. A preference point is a place in line for a general deer tag.

How you get points

You earn a point when you apply for a permit and don't draw, or when you apply for a point only. You can't apply for a permit and a point for the same species in the same draw.

  • License first. You need a valid Utah hunting or combination license to apply for a permit or a point. For ages 18–64, a hunting license is $40 for residents and $144 for nonresidents.
  • Point-only codes. On the application you pick the species' bonus point code (for limited-entry deer it's DEE) or the general-season deer preference point code (GDR).
  • Cost. A point costs the same as an application: $10 for residents and $21 for nonresidents, plus a 2.2% card transaction fee.
  • Two windows. The main window ran March 19 to April 23, 2026. If you missed it, you could buy a point during the antlerless application period, June 9–23, 2026.
  • Age. You must be 12 to hunt big game. An 11-year-old can apply if they turn 12 by December 31 of the hunt year.

Points are tracked by species, not by unit. A bull elk bonus point works for any future limited-entry bull elk hunt, and a general deer preference point works for any general-season deer hunt choice.

How bonus points work in the draw (elk and limited-entry deer)

Utah's rule (R657-62-8) sets the mechanics:

  1. Half to the top point holders. 50% of the permits for each hunt are reserved for applicants with the most bonus points. The draw fills them starting at the highest point level and works down. Within a point level, random numbers break ties.
  2. Half at random, weighted by points. Every applicant gets one random number for the application plus one more for each bonus point. Someone with 6 points holds 7 numbers. Your best number is the one that counts. Unused reserved permits roll into this random half.
  3. Residents and nonresidents are drawn separately. Choices are evaluated separately for residents and nonresidents first. Leftover permits can then cross over between the two pools.

The draw order runs limited-entry buck deer, then bull elk, then pronghorn, then once-in-a-lifetime species, then general-season buck deer. You can only get one buck deer and one bull elk permit a year. If you draw limited-entry deer, you're dropped from the general deer draw and get a general deer preference point instead.

Groups: Up to four hunters can apply together for limited-entry deer or elk. Bonus points are averaged and rounded down, so a 12-point hunter with a 0-point friend applies at 6. Groups aren't allowed for once-in-a-lifetime or management bull elk hunts.

How preference points work (general-season buck deer)

General deer is a pure preference draw. You list up to five hunt choices. The draw looks at every first choice at the highest point level, then the next level down, and so on, before it moves to second choices. Drawing any general deer permit, from any choice, resets your preference points to zero. Buying a leftover general buck permit after the draw also costs you your points (youth over-the-counter archery is an exception).

Twenty percent of general-season buck deer permits are set aside for youth (17 and under on July 31). Groups of up to four can apply, with points averaged and rounded down.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Nonresident permit numbers are set for each hunt. In the 2026 bull elk tables, for example, the Manti unit had 593 resident and 67 nonresident permits. On small hunts, that can mean one or two nonresident permits, so the max-point half might be a single tag.

Keeping and losing points

  • You lose points when you draw. Drawing a permit for a species, in or after the draw, wipes your points for that species. Conservation, expo, sportsman and landowner/CWMU-voucher permits don't cost you points.
  • Surrendering late. If you surrender a permit less than 30 days before the season, you lose your points for that species. In a group, everyone loses them.
  • No use-it-or-lose-it rule today. Current Utah rules don't take points for skipping years. An older rule that forfeited bonus points after three years without applying was repealed in 2012. You can sit out a year without losing anything. Applying or buying a point each year is still the only way to add points.
  • Waiting periods. After you draw a limited-entry, CWMU or management buck deer or bull elk permit, you wait five years before you can apply again for that species. Once-in-a-lifetime means exactly that. General-season permits have no waiting period.
  • Separate species. Elk bonus points, limited-entry deer bonus points and general deer preference points are all separate.

Point creep and "points to draw"

"Points to draw" is the point level where the max-point half of a hunt ran out last year. In Utah's bonus system, that number creeps up when more people build points than there are permits. Below that level, you are playing the random half.

Elk example: Say a limited-entry rifle bull hunt has 20 resident permits. Ten go to max points. If 40 residents sit at the top point level, a lucky 10 of them draw, and everyone else falls into the random half for the other 10. A 4-point hunter in that random half holds five numbers. That's better than one, but still a long shot. DWR's 2022 figures showed resident odds as good as about 1 in 2 on some units and worse than 1 in 60 on the hardest.

Deer example: In the 2025 general-season draw, nearly every resident with 4 points drew. Some archery units drew with 0 points, and some popular rifle units took 3–4. Nonresidents with 10 or more points all drew.

Strategy

  • If you want a trophy elk unit, buy a bonus point every year. At $10 or $21 plus a license, it's the cheapest part of a Utah plan. Use the random half as your lottery ticket while you climb.
  • Hunt while you wait. General-season any-bull and spike elk permits are sold over the counter. See general-season elk permits.
  • Use your five general deer choices. Put the unit you want first and a low-demand archery hunt lower down.
  • CWMUs and outfitters. Nonresidents can't draw CWMU permits, but CWMU operators sell vouchers, usually as guided hunts, and those don't use or cost points. See hunting leases and discount guided hunts.

Pick Utah, elk or deer, and your points to see how long a hunt might take.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Do I lose my Utah points if I skip a year? No. Current rules only take points when you draw (or surrender a permit late). Skipping just means you don't add one.

Can I apply for limited-entry deer and general deer in the same year? Yes. If you draw limited-entry deer, you're left out of the general deer draw and get a general deer preference point.

Does a group help my odds? No. Points are averaged and rounded down, so a group usually hurts the high-point member.
