title: Washington Special Permit Points Explained (Elk & Deer)
excerpt: How Washington's squared-point special permit drawing works for elk and deer: buying your license first, application fees, permit categories, points per category, groups and real odds for residents and nonresidents.
content:
Washington runs a squared bonus point lottery. Every special permit you apply for earns one point in that permit category, and in the drawing your points are squared to set how many "names in the hat" you get. Three points means nine chances; ten points means 100. There is no slice of permits reserved for the top point holders, so a first-year applicant can draw a hunt that someone else has waited a decade for. More points help a lot, but nothing is ever guaranteed.

The other thing to know up front: special permits are extras. Every resident and nonresident can buy a general season deer or elk tag over the counter. The drawing is for hunts on top of that, like quality bull and buck hunts, antlerless hunts and second deer tags.

How you get points

You earn a point by buying a special permit application in a category. That's it. There is no separate "preference point" product.

  • Apply and don't draw: one point in that category.
  • Point Saver: you can buy the application and choose the points-only option instead of listing hunts. If you buy an application and never submit hunt choices, WDFW still assigns you a points-option entry and you get the point.
  • Cost: a points-only application costs the same as a regular one ($9.61 resident, $152.30 nonresident in 2026; quality categories are $18.72 for residents).
  • License first: for deer and elk, you must buy your hunting license and choose your general season transport tag (weapon and area) before WDFW will sell you an application. For a nonresident, that means paying for the full deer or elk license just to build a point.
  • Age: youth categories are for hunters under 16 when they buy the application and license. The 65-and-over categories require you to turn 65 during the license year.

How points are used in the draw

WDFW's drawing is a weighted random draw. WDFW describes each hunter's points as squared to set their number of "names in the hat." As WDFW staff demonstrated the 2025 draw (reported by Northwest Sportsman), the computer gives each hunter that many random numbers, and the best (lowest) one sets their rank. Hunters are then processed in rank order through their hunt choices, in the priority order they listed.

What that means in practice:

  • One weighted pool. WDFW's rules describe a single weighted point selection system. They don't set aside a top-points pool or a separate random pool.
  • No nonresident quota in the rules. WDFW's special permit rules don't set a nonresident quota, so residents and nonresidents go into the same drawing. The difference is cost.
  • Choices: list up to four hunts on a regular application and up to two on a Quality application. A hunter who misses on the first choice can still land the second, third or fourth if permits remain when their rank comes up.
  • Groups: up to eight hunters for deer or elk (two for multi-season). All members' points are averaged, everyone must be eligible for the hunts listed, and if the group draws, everyone gets a permit. A group can't be larger than the number of permits in a hunt.

Points are per category, not per species

This is the part that trips people up. Washington tracks points separately for each permit category. You can apply in each category you qualify for, once per year, and each one builds its own point total.

Multi-season deer and elk tags are drawn separately, through their own application that runs from December through March 31. A Second Deer permit also needs a second deer tag using the same weapon as your first.

Points can't be moved between categories or given to another hunter.

Residents vs. nonresidents

For a nonresident, a single elk application really costs $685.60 plus $152.30, or $837.90, before any processing fee. Two categories (say, Quality Elk and Bull Elk) add another $152.30. The good news is that the license also lets you hunt the general season with the tag you picked.

Keeping and losing points

  • Drawing resets to zero. Your points in that category go to zero when you're drawn, whether or not you fill the tag.
  • Returning a permit: if you can't hunt, return the permit at least two weeks before the season opens and WDFW restores your points to where they were. Call (360) 902-2515.
  • Lapses: WDFW's current rules don't spell out a point expiration for skipped years. Apply every year anyway; a year off is a year of points you don't earn.
  • Waiting periods: none for deer and elk categories. (Moose, bighorn ram and mountain goat are once-in-a-lifetime harvests.)
  • Elk and deer are separate, and so is every category within them.

Point creep and what "points to draw" means

In a squared system there's no hard number of points that guarantees a permit. Instead, the more points the hunters around you hold, the less each of your entries is worth. Popular categories fill with hunters sitting on high point totals, and their squared entries swamp the field. That's point creep, Washington style.

Real 2025 numbers from WDFW's draw, as reported by Northwest Sportsman: about 12,500 hunters submitted Second Deer applications for 2,272 antlerless permits, so on paper a bit better than one in six overall. Some of those hunts didn't even fill; on Orcas Island, only 80 of 135 permits were awarded, and most winners had one point.

Elk example (hypothetical): a hunter with 9 points has 81 entries; a hunter with 3 points has 9. In a Quality Elk hunt with thousands of applicants and a handful of permits, both are long shots, but the 9-point hunter is nine times as likely to rank high.

Deer example (hypothetical): in an antlerless or Second Deer hunt with more permits than serious applicants, a 1-point hunter can draw on the first try. Those hunts don't reward patience as much as reading the hunt list.

Strategy

  • Hunt the general season every year. Your license is already paid for. Treat special permits as bonuses.
  • Apply in more than one category. Bull Elk, Antlerless Elk and Quality Elk are separate draws with separate points. Residents pay little to apply in several.
  • Nonresidents: decide if you're coming. Since you must buy the full license to apply, Washington points make the most sense if you plan to hunt the general season anyway.
  • Look for undersubscribed hunts. Antlerless, Second Deer and some youth and senior hunts sometimes go unfilled.
  • Check access. Some permit hunts are on private timberland where owners limit access or charge fees.
  • Raffles and auctions run outside the point system.
  • Private ground and guides. An outfitter with access can turn a general season tag into a solid hunt. See hunting leases and discount guided hunts.

Key numbers for 2026

FAQ

Can I build points without buying a license? Not for deer or elk. The license and transport tag come first.

Do my Bull Elk points count toward Quality Elk? No. Each category has its own points.

Can a first-time applicant draw? Yes. Buying the application earns your first point, so you go into the ranking with at least one entry, and new hunters draw every year, especially in antlerless and Second Deer hunts.

Are nonresidents capped? WDFW's special permit rules don't set a nonresident quota; the barrier is price.

What if I draw and can't go? Return the permit at least two weeks before the opener to get your points back.

title: Wyoming Preference Points Explained (Elk & Deer)
excerpt: How Wyoming's elk and deer preference points work: the nonresident 75/25 preference and random split, special vs. regular price draws, buying points, fees, the resident random draw, and 2026 key numbers.
content:
Wyoming uses a preference point system for nonresidents only, with a random draw on the side. In each hunt area and license type, 75% of nonresident licenses go to the applicants with the most points and 25% are drawn at random. Residents don't use points for elk or deer. Their limited quota licenses are drawn at random, and resident general licenses are sold over the counter. For a nonresident, that means points are the reliable route to a good tag, but the random pool gives anyone a real chance any year, even with zero points.

How you get points

This is where Wyoming differs from most states: nonresidents build elk and deer points by buying them. WGFD's rules say points are accumulated by purchasing a preference point during the point purchase period. Don't count on getting a point just for applying and missing.

  • When: July 1 to November 2, 2026, through WGFD's online license system.
  • Cost (2026): $52 for elk and $41 for deer ($10 for youth).
  • Cost from 2027: The Game and Fish Commission voted in April 2026 to raise nonresident points to $75 each for elk and deer, effective January 1, 2027. Points bought during the July to November 2026 window are listed at the 2026 prices.
  • Limit: One point per species per year.
  • Who can buy: You can't buy a point for a species in a year you drew your first choice in the initial draw.
  • Youth: Must be at least 11 when buying and turn 12 by December 31 that year.
  • No license required first. Wyoming has no qualifying license. The point is a stand-alone purchase.

How points are used in the draw

Only your first choice uses points. You can list three choices. Your points count only for your first choice in the preference draw.

The 75/25 split. For each hunt area and license type:

  1. 75% of licenses go through the preference point draw. Applicants are ranked by points, highest first. Everyone takes part, including people with zero points.
  2. 25% go to a random draw. Everyone who missed in the preference draw is entered, regardless of points. Points don't add any extra chances in the random draw.

Regular vs. special price. Wyoming holds back 40% of nonresident elk and deer licenses for special price applicants, who pay an extra fee:

Special and regular applicants draw in completely separate pools. Each has its own 75% preference draw and 25% random draw. Fewer people pay the special price, so the same hunt often takes fewer points at special price. Your points work in either pool.

Parties. Up to six hunters can apply together. They must all pick the same draw (regular or special), hunt area, and license type. For nonresident elk and deer, the party's points are averaged (to four decimal places). The party shares one random number, so applying together doesn't improve your odds. Residents and nonresidents can't apply together.

Doe/fawn and cow/calf licenses don't use or earn points.

Residents vs. nonresidents

Nonresident share. In a 2021 explainer, WGFD described limited quota elk licenses as split 84% resident and 16% nonresident; check the current regulations for this year's split. Nonresident licenses are allocated first, with 40% to special and 60% to regular, and any nonresident licenses that go unused go to the resident draw. Nonresident region general elk licenses fall under a statewide nonresident elk cap set by Commission rule.

WGFD charges the full license fee when you apply and refunds it if you don't draw. The application fee isn't refunded.

Keeping and losing points

  • Drawing your first choice in the initial draw wipes out all your points for that species.
  • Drawing a second or third choice doesn't cost your points.
  • Two-year rule: You lose all your points for a species if you don't buy a point for two consecutive years. Applying alone isn't enough to protect them.
  • No waiting period after drawing elk or deer.
  • Separate by species. Elk and deer points are separate, and so are the prices and deadlines.

Elk vs. deer: the differences that matter

  • Deadlines: Nonresident elk closes in early winter (February 2 in 2026). Deer closes June 1, the same as residents.
  • Point price: $52 elk vs. $41 deer in 2026. Both go to $75 in 2027.
  • Regions: Nonresident elk has three region general licenses (Eastern, Southern, Western). Deer has many lettered regions with very different demand.
  • Point levels: Elk region general licenses took a few points in 2026. Deer ranges from zero-point regions to Region G and H, which take as many points as many limited quota elk areas.

Point creep and "points to draw"

WGFD's demand reports show how many applicants at each point level drew each hunt. "Points to draw" is the lowest level that drew in the preference pool. As nonresidents keep buying points, popular hunts drift upward. That's point creep. The top point level in 2026 was 20.

Elk example (2026 nonresident draw). Regular price Western Region general took 6 points to draw for certain. At special price, it was 100% at 5 points, and some applicants drew at 4. A regular applicant with 3 points was really relying on the 25% random draw.

Deer example (2026 nonresident draw). Region G at regular price took 12 points for certain, and Region H took 9. At special price, G took 10 and H took 7. Several other regions drew at 0 to 3 points.

These tiers are our summary of WGFD's 2026 demand reports, not official WGFD categories, and next year's numbers will differ.

Strategy

  • Buy points every year you might want to hunt. Since points come only by purchase and lapse after two missed years, set a reminder for July.
  • Use the random pool. With 25% of licenses drawn at random, a zero-point application for a premium area is a long-shot lottery ticket.
  • Weigh special price. Paying the special price can save you two or three years of points on a region general license. On easy deer regions it often isn't needed.
  • Don't burn points on an easy first choice. If your first choice draws at zero points, you lose everything you've built.
  • Add doe/fawn or cow/calf licenses. These don't touch your points.
  • Outfitters and private land. Nonresidents hunting federal wilderness need a licensed outfitter or a resident guide. Private-land access is worth a look too: see hunting leases and discount guided hunts.

FAQ

Do I get a point if I apply and don't draw? Plan on buying it. WGFD's rules say nonresident elk and deer points come from buying a point between July 1 and November 2.

Do my points carry between regular and special? Yes. Points belong to the species, not the price type. You use them in whichever draw you apply for.

Do residents need points? No. Wyoming residents have no elk or deer preference points. Limited quota licenses are drawn at random.
